data.title: Survey: Shoppers to use AI for holiday season — including autonomous purchases
data.ai_summary: A Forter survey found 67% of consumers plan to use AI for holiday shopping, with 37% expecting more use than last year. 43% discovered or purchased from a new retailer via AI recommendations, and 53% would let AI make autonomous gift purchases.
data.full_text:
Survey: Shoppers to use AI for holiday season — including autonomous purchases

A majority of respondents said they are comfortable letting AI handle at least one part of their holiday shopping journey Artificial intelligence tools are being quickly adopted by consumers – especially with the holidays around the corner. The majority (67%) of consumers say they plan to use AI to help with holiday shopping this year, according to a new survey from e-commerce platform Forter. More than a third (37%) of holiday shoppers expect to use it more than last year. Notably, 43% of those surveyed said they have already discovered or purchased from a retailer they had never shopped with before because of an AI recommendation. [READ MORE: Survey: Consumers leverage AI tools to compare prices, find discounts ] More than three-quarters (78%) of respondents said they are comfortable letting AI handle at least one part of their holiday shopping journey. More than half (53%) would be comfortable letting AI purchase a holiday gift autonomously, depending on the purchase amount.

data.title: Skyfire, Forter partner on agentic commerce checkout | The Paypers
data.ai_summary: Forter now accepts Skyfire's Know Your Agent tokens, adding agent identity data to fraud decisions on agentic purchases. The integration raised Jomashop's agentic checkout success rate to nearly 100% without increased chargebacks. The companies see it as an early model for identity-first checkout as agentic commerce grows.
data.author: Claudia Pincovski
data.full_text:
AI agents shopping on behalf of real customers often look like bots to traditional bot management tools, which were built to flag non-human browsing and high automation signals. US-based Skyfire and Forter have expanded their partnership to address this. Forter now accepts Skyfire’s Know Your Agent (KYA) tokens, adding agent identity data to its fraud decisions on agentic purchases. The companies report higher checkout success rates on agentic traffic without additional risk.
Separating trusted agents from malicious automation
According to the companies, legacy bot controls block checkouts for genuine agentic traffic, leading to lost revenue. At the same time, fraudsters are trying to exploit agentic commerce by posing as legitimate agents, while AI platforms can mask identity signals. The integration builds on Forter’s Fraud Management for Agentic Commerce capabilities, which now ingest Skyfire’s KYA protocol data. The added signals come as agentic orders across Forter’s network have increased more than fourfold since August 2026.
For Forter merchants, the integration is intended to raise authorisation rates and reduce chargeback exposure, while legitimate agent purchases complete without added friction. The checkout interface does not change, as the new agentic signals pass alongside existing risk data. Eran Vanounou, Chief Technology and Product Officer at Forter, said agentic commerce fails if retailers cannot tell an authorised buyer from a script imitating one, and the combined approach validates both the AI agent and the underlying consumer.
Jomashop pilot and implications for merchants
The partnership was piloted with Jomashop, a US-based online retailer of watches, jewellery, and accessories. Jomashop had seen bot management tools block much of its agentic traffic, and during the pilot its agentic checkout success rate rose to nearly 100% without an increase in chargebacks. Osher Karnowsky, General Manager of Jomashop.com, said the integration helps the retailer understand who the agent is, who sent it, and whether to trust the transaction.
For agentic commerce platforms, the integration removes the default penalty applied to agent transactions. Craig DeWitt, Co-Founder and Head of Product at Skyfire, said current fraud and security systems were not built to recognise AI agents, and integrating KYA identity into Forter’s decisioning lets merchants separate authorised agents from malicious bots. The companies see the partnership as an early model for identity-first checkout as more commerce traffic comes from software acting for consumers.

data.title: Money20/20 USA day one: Las Vegas asks who is holding the bag | The Fintech Times
data.ai_summary: Money20/20 USA day one in Las Vegas focused on stablecoin and agent risk, with Mastercard launching Stablecoin Security, a risk score combining fraud and blockchain analytics. Panels highlighted the need for trust before scale, citing stablecoin adoption gaps and agent identity verification. Mastercard expects one in ten transactions by an agent by 2030.
data.author: Amrit Kang

industries.name: Risk Scoring, Credit & Fraud Analytics (counterparty/wallet risk)

data.full_text:
Day one in Las Vegas on the stablecoin and agent stages. Every panel I sat in kept circling one question: when money moves itself, who carries the risk?
I spent Monday, the first full day of Money20/20 USA at The Venetian, moving between the Meridian and Intersection stages with a recorder running. By the afternoon I could have written the same sentence under every session. Nobody I heard was still arguing about whether stablecoins or AI agents work. The argument was about who carries the risk when they do something nobody intended.
Trust before scale
It started with Mastercard. Just before its late-morning stablecoin panel, Ann Johnson, who runs security solutions at Mastercard, launched Stablecoin Security, a risk score for stablecoin payments that combines 16 years of the network’s fraud, identity and cyber intelligence with blockchain analytics and is built to work at machine speed. Her framing was simple: “the thing that allows innovation to scale is trust.” Mastercard says it will launch in North America first, with worldwide availability expected in 2027.
The panel that followed made the case for why it is needed. Rajpal Khangura, co-founder and chief compliance officer of Keyrails, settles trade payments for merchants in markets such as Nigeria paying suppliers in China, with an average ticket of $250,000 to $350,000. His customers used to ask only how cheap and how fast; now they ask how safe the wallet is, and how safe the fiat is when it lands. His hardest problem is the wallet that is not sanctioned itself but has transacted a few hops away from one that is, and keeping his own risk appetite in step with every bank and liquidity partner downstream. He also told the room it can still be quicker to put cash in the back of a van and drive it across a border than to send the payment.
Keith Vander Leest, who runs BVNK in the US and is now part of Mastercard, said too much stablecoin activity is still trading and he wants real-world payments to become the majority. That, in his view, depends on building quickly the protections the fiat world took decades to build, and on carrying far more data with each payment on chain, from ISO 20022 messages to travel rule information. Alex Garn of Borderless said the US can learn from instant payments in the UK, where extra checks happen at the moment a new payee is added, and from Pix in Brazil, where fraud is fought by sharing signals across the whole network rather than bank by bank. His one-word answer to what the industry must get right was invisible.
The enterprise view
Earlier that morning, on the Intersection Stage, Nik Milanović of This Week in Fintech chaired From Pilot to Payout, a panel with Payoneer, eBay and Citi. He opened with Payoneer’s new survey of 265 payments, treasury and finance leaders, in which 69 per cent are already using stablecoins and 41 per cent at meaningful scale, then asked the room who had actually paid with one. I counted six or seven hands, in a room full of payments professionals.
The panel explained the gap. Renata Camera Santos, head of wallet at eBay, said a marketplace has to give buyers and sellers the same experience whatever the rail, and that solving for the happy path is not enough when card payments have had decades to work through every edge case. Every vendor pitches stablecoins as if the world is your oyster, Santos said, when what a marketplace needs is to be told where the oyster is. Pix in Brazil, where Santos grew up, already delivers much of what stablecoins promise, so a stablecoin has to fix a margin or speed problem better than that.
Will Artingstall, Citi’s head of banking as a service, said that for the first time a new-product conversation with clients was about risk rather than features, with a new vocabulary of know-your-transaction checks and hosted and unhosted wallets, and that the dispute rights a card holder takes for granted have no stablecoin equivalent yet. Where Citi has seen strong take-up is tokenised deposits, because clients fund from an ordinary account and never hold a wallet while the token is minted and burned behind the scenes. Rowland Berry of Payoneer added that however much of the stack you outsource, the accountability stays with whoever holds the licence.
Agents need papers
The afternoon session on the trust layer for agentic commerce, with Mastercard, Skyfire and Forter, was the most useful half hour of my day. Ranjita Iyer, executive vice president of services for North America at Mastercard, chaired it and said the network expects one transaction in ten could be made by an agent by 2030, possibly sooner. Adam Davies, director of AI strategy at Forter, set out what a merchant now has to establish for every agent at the door: which person it represents, whether it is acting within the authority it was given, and what credential it is paying with. Each already has rival standards, from Visa‘s Trusted Agent Protocol and Google’s AP2 to Mastercard’s Verifiable Intent and Stripe‘s shared payment tokens, and no merchant can realistically support them all alone.
Amir Sarhangi of Skyfire said we built the internet for humans and today’s fraud tools are probabilistic, while merchants now want to know with certainty which agents are good and who is behind them. Skyfire’s Know Your Agent token binds a verified business behind an agent to verified details of its user, and Forter reads it at checkout. Merchants, he said, do not want a separate registration for agents; they want the agent recognised as the customer it acts for, loyalty account and all.
Then Iyer raised the question that has followed this whole autumn of conferences. When an agent buys something its owner did not authorise, or simply gets it wrong, the issuer needs that identity and intent data to deal with the liability and, in Iyer’s words, “to figure out who’s holding the bag on those types of transactions.”
Rules after innovation
I finished on the Intersection Stage with former CFTC Chairman J. Christopher Giancarlo, a month after the CLARITY Act failed a Senate procedural vote. He was relaxed about it. “As someone who wrote rules at the CFTC, I’m not that disappointed that clarity didn’t get done,” he said, arguing that the US should let innovation solve commercial problems first and legislate once the public policy issues are clear, as his old agency is now doing with prediction markets. He predicted that by 2040 anything of value that can be tokenised will be.
Karin Kusano, the crypto strategist known as Cryptomommi, gave the session its human side, describing how ordinary banking shut her out when she had no fixed address. She then turned on her own industry: crypto has behaved like a teenager, she said, and needs to grow up, starting with pump-and-dump schemes and meme coins.
Around the floor
Elsewhere on Monday, Huntington launched The 1866 Studio, an agentic small business platform built with Google Cloud, Proof and Circle demonstrated an agent proving who it acts for and then paying in USDC, and Skyfire and Forter formalised the partnership discussed on stage. Day two brings FDIC Chairman Travis Hill in conversation with the Financial Technology Association at 10:00 Pacific time.

data.title: Two-Thirds of U.S. Consumers Plan to Shop with AI This Holiday Season, New Forter Research Finds
data.ai_summary: Forter's survey of 2,017 Americans found 67% plan to use AI for holiday shopping, with 43% having discovered or purchased from a new retailer via AI recommendation. Younger consumers (83%) are more likely than older ones (40%) to use AI, and 78% are comfortable letting AI handle part of the shopping journey.
data.author: Forter
data.full_text:
Forty-three percent have discovered or purchased from a new retailer based on an AI recommendation NEW YORK, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Two-thirds of U.S. consumers (67%) plan to use AI for holiday shopping this year, according to new consumer research released today by Forter, the Trust Intelligence platform for the future of commerce. The study of more than 2,000 Americans, conducted by The Harris Poll on Forter's behalf, revealed AI usage will surge ahead of the holidays. Polled a week after the launch of Meta's new personal AI assistant Muse, the majority of Americans (67%) say they plan to use AI to help with holiday shopping this year, with 37% of holiday shoppers expecting to use it more than last year. AI's influence on shopping behavior is apparent, with 43% of Americans having already discovered or purchased from a retailer they had never shopped with before because of an AI recommendation. "I've spent 25 years watching consumer behavior shift, from online to mobile to social, and each time retailers had months, sometimes years to adapt. With personal AI agents like Muse and Instinct, that timeline is a matter of months, if not weeks," said Jen Howard, chief merchant, Forter. "Our research shows that shoppers are already using AI to find deals, discover new brands, and even check out. This traffic is arriving at merchants' sites this holiday whether or not they're ready." The research also found a generational adoption curve. Among 18- to 34-years-olds, 83% plan to use AI for holiday shopping this year, compared with 40% of Americans 65 and older; and 68% have already discovered or purchased from a new retailer because of an AI recommendation, compared with just 13% of Americans 65+. Consumers are comfortable delegating parts of the shopping journey to agents, but maintaining control remains a priority. Seventy-eight percent of holiday shoppers say they're comfortable letting AI handle at least one part of their holiday shopping journey, and 53% would be comfortable letting AI purchase a holiday gift autonomously, depending on the purchase amount. When asked what would make them more comfortable with autonomous transactions for holiday gifts, holiday shoppers cited the need for greater control and protection, including: Requiring final approval before purchase (26%)

Setting spending limits (24%)

Guaranteeing a refund if AI buys the wrong item (23%) or completes a fraudulent transaction (22%),

transaction (22%), Controlling what personal data AI can access (22%). "Many shoppers are ready to hand AI the keys, but not without guardrails. They want final approval, spending limits, and a guarantee they'll be made whole if something goes wrong," said Howard. "Retailers that design for that now will be the ones AI agents, and the shoppers behind them, choose to buy from." For more information about the research, visit: forter.com/blog/ai-holiday-shopping-us-survey/. About Forter Forter delivers trust intelligence and payments infrastructure built for the commerce moments that matter. Powered by a global identity network, our AI makes instant trust decisions from sign-up to checkout to returns — so every trusted customer always gets the experience they deserve. Nordstrom, Instacart, Priceline, and nearly 1 million businesses trust Forter to keep the right customers coming back. Zero friction for the customers who matter. No revenue left behind. Learn more at Forter.com. Survey Method: This survey was conducted online within the United States by The Harris Poll on behalf of Forter from September 15-16, 2026 among 2,017 adults ages 18 and older, among whom 1,927 plan to shop for holiday gifts. The sampling precision of Harris online polls is measured by using a Bayesian credible interval. For this study, the sample data is accurate to within +/- 2.7 percentage points using a 95% confidence level. For complete survey methodology, including weighting variables and subgroup sample sizes, please contact [email protected]. SOURCE Forter, Inc.

data.title: Skyfire and Forter Enrich Trusted Agentic Commerce Decisions at Checkout
data.ai_summary: Skyfire and Forter announced a partnership integrating Skyfire's Know Your Agent (KYA) tokens into Forter's fraud decisioning, increasing agentic checkout success rates without added risk. The integration was piloted with Jomashop, which saw its agentic checkout success rate rise to nearly 100% without increasing chargebacks. The partnership aims to distinguish trusted agents from malicious bots as agentic commerce grows.
data.full_text:
Skyfire and Forter Enrich Trusted Agentic Commerce Decisions at Checkout Provided by Business Wire

Skyfire and Forter Enrich Trusted Agentic Commerce Decisions at Checkout Forter accepts Skyfire’s Know Your Agent (KYA) tokens, lifting checkout success rates on agentic purchases, without introducing additional risk Skyfire, the Agent Trust Stack, and Forter, the Trust Intelligence Platform for the future of commerce, today announced their strengthened partnership which has successfully increased checkout success rates on agentic traffic, without introducing additional risk. Traditional bot management solutions were built to flag non-human browsing behavior and high automation signals, which are exactly the characteristics of legitimate AI agents acting on behalf of real customers. The result is blocked checkouts for genuine agentic traffic and lost revenue. At the same time, fraudsters are actively looking for opportunities to exploit agentic commerce by masking as legitimate agents, making it challenging for merchants to know who to trust, especially when identity signals can be masked by AI platforms. Together, Skyfire and Forter are solving this problem by distinguishing trusted agents from malicious automation. The integration builds on Forter’s existing Fraud Management for Agentic Commerce capabilities, which now ingests Skyfire’s KYA protocol data to enrich decisioning on agentic purchases. This added layer of intelligence comes as agentic orders across Forter's network have increased more than fourfold since August. For Forter merchants, the partnership will enable delivery of higher authorization rates and reduction in chargeback exposure while enabling legitimate agent purchases to be completed without any additional friction. Nothing changes at the checkout UI. The new agentic signals pass alongside existing risk data. The partnership was successfully piloted with Jomashop, the Brooklyn-based online retailer of luxury watches, jewelry, and accessories. Jomashop strengthened its agentic checkout success rates, where bot management tools blocked much of the traffic, to nearly 100% success rate, without increasing chargebacks. "Our customers are starting to shop through agents, and we didn’t want to be the reason a legitimate purchase was declined. With Skyfire and Forter working together, we can better understand who the agent is, who sent it, and whether to trust the transaction,” said Osher Karnowsky, General Manager, Jomashop.com. “That clarity gives us confidence to support agentic buyers without introducing additional risk to the business." For agentic commerce platforms, the integration will remove the structural penalty applied to agent transactions by default. For the broader ecosystem, the partnership sets an early template for what identity-first checkout looks like in an era where a growing share of commerce traffic originates from software acting on behalf of a person. Eran Vanounou, Chief Technology and Product Officer at Forter, said the partnership addresses where ecosystem friction is hitting hardest. “Agentic commerce fails if retailers can’t tell the difference between an authorized buyer and a script trying to look like one,” Vanounou said. “Leveraging Forter and Skyfire lets businesses confidently validate both the identity of the AI agent and the trustworthiness of the underlying consumer. We are empowering digital commerce leaders to welcome AI-driven purchases while protecting their bottom line from fraud.” Craig DeWitt, Co-Founder and Head of Product at Skyfire, said the integration removes one of the biggest barriers to scaling agentic commerce. “AI agents represent an entirely new channel for commerce, but today's fraud and security systems weren't built to recognize them,” DeWitt said. “By integrating Skyfire's Know Your Agent (KYA) identity directly into Forter's fraud decisioning, we're giving merchants the ability to distinguish trusted, authorized agents from malicious bots. This is a critical step toward making agentic commerce as secure, seamless, and scalable as traditional online shopping.” About Skyfire Skyfire is the trust layer for agentic commerce, providing identity and payment infrastructure for AI agents. Through its open Know Your Agent (KYA) protocol, Skyfire gives AI and agents everything they need to transact autonomously, including verified identity for web access and account creation, tokenized credit cards, real-time micropayments, and instant programmatic checkout. Through KYA, platforms can enable agents to sign up, authenticate, and transact across APIs, websites, and marketplaces at scale. The company is backed by Evolution and DCVC, a16z CSX, Coinbase Ventures, Neuberger Berman, Brevan Howard Digital, and other leading investors. Learn more at skyfire.xyz. About Forter Forter delivers trust intelligence and payments infrastructure built for the commerce moments that matter. Powered by a global identity network, our AI makes instant trust decisions from sign-up to checkout to returns — so every trusted customer always gets the experience they deserve. Nordstrom, Instacart, Priceline, and nearly 1 million businesses trust Forter to keep the right customers coming back. Zero friction for the customers who matter. No revenue left behind. Craig DeWitt, Co-Founder and Head of Product at Skyfire, said the integration removes one of the biggest barriers to scaling agentic commerce. “AI agents represent an entirely new channel for commerce, but today's fraud and security systems weren't built to recognize them,” DeWitt said. “By integrating Skyfire's Know Your Agent (KYA) identity directly into Forter's fraud decisioning, we're giving merchants the ability to distinguish trusted, authorized agents from malicious bots. This is a critical step toward making agentic commerce as secure, seamless, and scalable as traditional online shopping.”

About Skyfire

Skyfire is the trust layer for agentic commerce, providing identity and payment infrastructure for AI agents. Through its open Know Your Agent (KYA) protocol, Skyfire gives AI and agents everything they need to transact autonomously, including verified identity for web access and account creation, tokenized credit cards, real-time micropayments, and instant programmatic checkout. Through KYA, platforms can enable agents to sign up, authenticate, and transact across APIs, websites, and marketplaces at scale. The company is backed by Evolution and DCVC, a16z CSX, Coinbase Ventures, Neuberger Berman, Brevan Howard Digital, and other leading investors. Learn more at skyfire.xyz.

About Forter

Forter delivers trust intelligence and payments infrastructure built for the commerce moments that matter. Powered by a global identity network, our AI makes instant trust decisions from sign-up to checkout to returns — so every trusted customer always gets the experience they deserve. Nordstrom, Instacart, Priceline, and nearly 1 million businesses trust Forter to keep the right customers coming back. Zero friction for the customers who matter. No revenue left behind. data.title: Mercari, Inc. has fully implemented Forter's AI judgment platform.
data.ai_summary: Mercari fully implemented Forter's AI judgment platform to combat fraudulent credit card transactions, working with GMO Payment Gateway. Preliminary verification showed chargebacks reduced to about one-tenth and credit card GMV improved. The solution integrates via GMO-PG's API, reducing development workload.
data.full_text: Forter GMO Payment Gateway, Inc. October 15, 2026 - Forter, a company providing an AI judgment platform for next-generation commerce (headquartered in New York, USA), and GMO Payment Gateway, Inc. (President: Kazunari Aihara, hereinafter referred to as GMO-PG), which is part of the GMO Internet Group, announced that Mercari, Inc. (headquartered in Minato-ku, Tokyo, CEO: Shintaro Yamada, hereinafter referred to as Mercari), which operates Japan's largest flea market app "Mercari," has fully introduced Forter's AI judgment platform as a measure against fraudulent credit card transactions. Forter and GMO-PG have jointly verified from the initial stage with Mercari, resulting in the introduction of Forter's AI judgment solution. Additionally, GMO-PG provides an API (Application Programming Interface) that standardly implements Forter's fraud detection function in its online comprehensive payment service "PG Multi-Payment Service." 1. Background of the Introduction: Mercari has implemented various fraud prevention measures to create a safe and secure environment for customers, including measures against fraudulent credit card transactions. Until now, they have applied 3D Secure (Note 1) to transactions deemed necessary for authentication based on their own rules and conducted visual checks on transactions deemed necessary for confirmation. However, as fraudulent methods have become more sophisticated, they faced challenges such as the degradation of the payment experience due to friction from 3D Secure (Note 2), increased chargebacks (Note 3), and rising human costs for fraud prevention. To balance "ensuring security" and "providing a smooth payment experience for genuine customers," the selection of a new fraud prevention solution was advanced. 2. Selection of Forter and Results of Preliminary Verification: In the preliminary verification conducted prior to full implementation, Forter demonstrated results exceeding the evaluation criteria set by Mercari in the following three areas: ① Reduction in the utilization rate of 3D Secure and improvement in credit card GMV (Note 4) Forter returns a judgment with three options: "OK (approved) / NG (rejected) / 3D Secure (recommended)" at the time of transaction request. With three options, merchants (Note 5) can avoid applying 3D Secure to low-risk transactions and focus recommendations on transactions that require judgment. Compliance with the mandatory introduction of EMV 3-D Secure (Note 6) is also automated within the same framework. In the preliminary verification, the utilization rate of 3D Secure decreased without expanding fraud risk, and credit card GMV improved. ② Chargeback amounts reduced to about one-tenth Forter has a global identity network (Note 7). It analyzes approximately 6,000 data attributes in real-time and assesses reliability for each transaction. Fraudulent methods evolve across borders. Therefore, Mercari emphasized the importance of a global data infrastructure that does not rely solely on its own data during the selection process. Although the chargeback occurrence rate was originally below the industry standard, it further improved in the preliminary verification. The chargeback amount was kept to about one-tenth of the level compared to the previous system. No incidents were observed where genuine transactions were mistakenly hindered for transactions judged as rejected. ③ Reduction of costs for visual confirmation and rule maintenance Forter updates AI models and responds in real-time to new fraudulent methods occurring globally. Therefore, merchants do not need to maintain rules on their side. Visual confirmation has also been automated, relieving Mercari of the burdensome manual tasks in fraud prevention. 3. Introduction through GMO-PG's Integrated API: This introduction utilizes the Forter integrated interface built on GMO-PG's "PG Multi-Payment Service." Since the entire flow from Forter's fraud detection request, application of 3D Secure based on judgment results, to payment processing is consolidated in GMO-PG's API, Mercari was able to introduce Forter as an extension of its existing payment integration. This eliminated the need for separate API connection development or infrastructure construction with Forter, leading to reduced development workload and shortened the period from the start of verification to actual operation. 4. Comments from Each Company: Mercari, Inc. Comment from Keisuke Tanaka, Executive Officer, VP of Customer Service / Trust and Safety Marketplace: "At Mercari, we prioritize creating an environment where everyone can conduct transactions safely and securely, and providing a smooth customer experience (UX) with minimal friction during payment. Until now, we have countered increasingly sophisticated fraudsters with our own fraud detection rules and risk-based judgments of 3D Secure, but we faced a dilemma with genuine customers experiencing 'cart abandonment.' In the preliminary verification conducted in strong partnership with GMO-PG and Forter, we achieved the result of reducing chargebacks to about one-tenth while improving the success rate of payments, thereby increasing credit card GMV. We are now completely free from tuning our own fraud detection rules and visual inspection tasks, and we are confident that we have built a solid payment infrastructure for scalable business development in the future." Comment from Yosuke Noda, Country Manager for Japan at Forter: "We are very pleased that Mercari, a representative of Japan's e-commerce, has adopted Forter as a partner responsible for enhancing security and customer experience in payments. The results demonstrated in this preliminary verification clearly show that our real-time judgments based on a global network of 2 billion users not only 'shut out fraud' but also 'remove friction and enhance GMV and sales.' We will continue to support Mercari in the 'thorough elimination' of fraudulent users and the enhancement of the 'core experience (Core CX)' during payments." Comment from Ryo Tanaka, Executive Officer at GMO Payment Gateway, Inc.: "As a Payment Service Provider (PSP) providing payment infrastructure to Mercari, and as a partner of Forter, we have jointly promoted this project from the initial stage. Balancing enhanced payment security with a smooth payment experience for buyers is a challenge faced by many e-commerce businesses. In this project, by combining Forter's real-time judgments with our payment system, we were able to achieve significant reductions in chargebacks while simultaneously improving GMV. We will continue to support Mercari's business growth through our alliance with both companies and contribute to the development of a safe and secure payment environment in Japan's e-commerce market." ===================================================================== About Mercari Mercari, Inc. is on a mission to "circulate all values and expand the possibilities of all people" and operates the flea market app "Mercari" in Japan and the US, promoting global expansion through cross-border business. By connecting individuals around the world through the power of technology, we aim to create a rich society where resources circulate and individuals can realize their aspirations. Furthermore, as a group, we are engaged in creating new value through financial services with Merpay, cryptocurrency-related businesses with Mercoin, and sports businesses through Kashima Antlers. About Forter Forter provides optimal AI judgments at every critical stage of commerce. Our proprietary AI, based on a global identity network, instantly assesses reliability from new registrations to payments and returns. Nearly 1 million businesses, including ZOZO, Ekinet, ASICS, and BEAMS, have adopted Forter to enhance the loyalty of quality customers. We provide a stress-free experience for important customers and ensure reliable revenue for businesses. data.title: Forter Turns the AI Shopping Agent Surge Into a Secure Revenue Channel for Merchants
data.ai_summary: Forter launched its Agentic Commerce Engine to help merchants verify AI shopping agents and enable secure headless checkout. Agentic orders on Forter's network have increased over fourfold since August, while automated fraud has doubled in two months. The engine is now available for all customers.
data.author: Forter
data.full_text:
Ahead of peak season, merchants can now identify trusted AI agents and enable secure, headless checkout with a single no-code integration NEW YORK, Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Forter, the Trust Intelligence platform for the future of commerce, introduced new capabilities designed to give commerce leaders the visibility, trust and control to securely embrace this rapidly emerging revenue channel. Forter's Agentic Commerce Engine enables merchants to verify agentic shoppers and provides the infrastructure to manage their end-to-end experience. Agentic orders across Forter's network have increased more than fourfold since August, while automated fraud has doubled in the last two months. Consumers are rapidly adopting AI personal assistants like Muse, Instinct and Grok Bot to search, compare and buy on their behalf. Bad actors are attempting to blend in to this traffic by using malicious agents or taking over legitimate ones to scale fraud and abuse. The ability to distinguish a trusted agent from a fraudulent one has never been more important. "Every merchant is now effectively opted in to agentic commerce, whether or not they've prepared for it," said Eran Vanounou, chief technology and product officer, Forter. "The choice merchants have isn't whether agentic traffic engages with their site this holiday season; it's whether they are equipped to control, optimize and drive revenue from it." Now available, Forter's Agentic Commerce Engine is the first complete solution for this channel combining trust intelligence with flexible infrastructure. The capabilities include: Fraud Management for Agentic Commerce identifies and decisions scraper- and agent-driven traffic in real time, distinguishing legitimate AI assistants from fraud and abuse bots. The capability is an extension of Forter's core Fraud Management offering and is now available for all customers.

The capability is an extension of Forter's core Management offering and is now available for all customers. Agentic Orchestration enables headless checkout via agentic protocols so that merchants can optimize how agents purchase and set the conditions for each transaction. Through a single, no-code Forter integration, merchants can manage the full checkout experience for AI agents.

enables headless checkout via agentic protocols so that merchants can optimize how agents purchase and set the conditions for each transaction. Through a single, no-code Forter integration, merchants can manage the full checkout experience for AI agents. AI Activity Dashboard shows merchants which AI agents are transacting on their site, so they can make informed decisions instead of guessing or blanket-blocking traffic that could represent new revenue. Merchants can analyze their transactions in the portal or with Forter Prism. Unlike the invite-only agentic pilots launched earlier this year, the new AI assistants can default to scraping a merchant's site when there isn't a headless checkout flow optimized for agents. Screen scraping is significantly slower, more costly and error-prone, negatively impacting the customer experience. In a controlled experiment, Forter found headless protocols were roughly 10 times faster and 5 times more token-efficient, and overall more likely to succeed, than scraping. Forter's Agentic Commerce Engine allows merchants to provide a superior customer buying experience by enabling headless checkout with a single integration. "There's a greater sense of urgency for agentic readiness as we head into peak season. Agentic traffic has had a meteoric rise over the last month and we expect that trend to continue," said Adam Davies, Director of AI, Forter. "We're giving merchants the intelligence and infrastructure to know which agentic transactions can be trusted and to control the end-to-end agentic shopping journey." Fraud Management for Agentic is now live for existing Forter customers. Agentic Orchestration is available now for interested Forter customers. For more information, visit https://www.forter.com/agentic-commerce. About Forter Forter delivers trust intelligence and payments infrastructure built for the commerce moments that matter. data.title: One in five Brits feel AI would choose better Xmas presents for them than partners Forter research — Retail Technology Innovation Hub
data.ai_summary: A Forter poll of 2,000 Brits found 22% would trust AI over a partner to pick Christmas gifts, citing access to more options and objective analysis. 53% of shoppers have used or are open to using AI for gifts, with 47% most likely to use it for a partner. The study also notes 43% cite finding well-received presents as the biggest festive stress point.
data.author: Scott Thompson
data.full_text: One in five Brits feel AI would choose better Xmas presents for them than partners Forter research Research More than a fifth of Brits would trust AI over their partner to pick a Christmas gift for them. A Forter poll of 2,000 people found 22% think the technology would know their likes and dislikes better than their other half. Among those convinced AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, would outperform a partner or loved one, 47% believe it’s because it could access more options. While 38% think it can analyse their interests more objectively and 36% note the technology remembers details about them better than their other half does. A further 29% think it knows and understands the trends they’re into more instinctively than anyone else. The research found that 53% of shoppers have used AI already, or are open to using it to find presents this Christmas. 23% of us receive an unwanted gift every year - most commonly from a family member (55%) whilst 12% have come to dread receiving disappointing presents, particularly from their partner. Of those set to use AI for their shopping this year, 47% said they would be most likely to use it when shopping for their partner, 25% would turn to it for gift ideas for a friend, and 24% for a sibling. Jennifer Howard, Chief Merchant at Forter, says: “The 'search bar' is starting to look old fashioned. People are asking AI to do the browsing, the comparing and the deciding for them. It's quietly becoming the nation's Secret Santa, less a shopping tool now and more a shopping companion.” “In fact, our research has found 39% of shoppers are more likely to buy from a retailer who has an AI agent to help with the purchasing journey and that nearly doubles to 63% among shoppers under 35 years old. Speed, convenience and security are still non-negotiables, especially during Christmas. Technology can spark the idea, but it's shoppers who'll decide how much of the actual buying they're ready to hand over to AI agents.” When asked what parts of the shopping process they would be comfortable letting AI tools handle fully autonomously, searching for gifts (42%) and selecting gifts (21%) came top. Others are inclined to let AI handle shipping (15%) and even buying gifts on their behalf (12%). The study found buying presents which would be well-received is the biggest festive stress point for 43% of us. In fact, 25% of those polled spend between three and five hours trying to find the perfect gifts, with a further 15% spending more than 10 hours. Meanwhile, 33% cited managing finances and food preparation among the most stressful aspects of the festive season. Among those using AI tools to relieve some of the pressure this year, 50% would use it for gift inspiration, while 46% would ask it to compare prices. 45% would use it to find deals and discounts and 29% would do so to create shopping lists and source festive recipes. Carried out via OnePoll, the study found 33% believe the biggest benefit of using AI this year will be the time it could save. While 29% think it will provide better gift ideas, a further 29% also said it could help them discover new products and brands. Technology topped the list of gift options which shoppers would trust AI to help discover or buy, selected by 32%, ahead of beauty products (26%), books (22%), and clothing (22%). In a ‘secret Santa’ move, 32% of those likely to use AI this Christmas admitted they wouldn’t reveal they’d utilised it regardless of whether the recipient liked the gift while 17% would only confess to using AI if the recipient did not like their gift. Howard says: “AI is increasingly being used as a personal shopping assistant. This changing consumer behaviour means brands that make themselves easy to discover and trust, whether via a search engine or AI tool, will be the ones that benefit most this gifting season.” 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards AI will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards . The awards are now open for entries and celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world. Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November. Check out our 2025 winners here . Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson . In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.” “But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.” He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.” Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering. data.full_text:
David’s Bridal enables digital fraud detection with help from AI

David's Bridal is fighting fraud. A leading bridal and special occasion dress retailer is beefing up its online anti-fraud efforts. David's Bridal is deploying the Forter artificial intelligence-based e-commerce decisioning platform to boost its ability to detect fraudulent online transactions without incorrectly flagging legitimate purchases. According to the retailer, bridal purchasing behavior — including customers who are one-time or infrequent purchasers, multiple shipping addresses tied to a single billing address and freight forwarders — can look like fraud to systems trained on conventional retail signals. The retailer selected Forter technology for its ability to distinguish fraud from legitimate bridal edge cases. Partnering with Chief Digital Agency (CDA) to implement the solution, David’s achieved a 99.78% approval rate during the first two weeks of launch, improving authorization performance while reducing friction for legitimate customers. "Every technology investment we make starts with one objective: creating a better experience for our guests while building a more agile business," said Scott Saeger, CTO at David's Bridal. data.title: Top International Chargeback Solutions for Cross-Border Ecommerce in 2026
data.ai_summary: The article reviews leading international chargeback solutions for cross-border ecommerce in 2026, highlighting platforms such as Chargeflow, Ethoca, and Verifi that help merchants manage disputes across multiple markets. It details how these tools utilize global card network alerts and automated evidence gathering to mitigate risks associated with unfamiliar fraud patterns and currency fluctuations. The piece also outlines key evaluation criteria for merchants, including data residency compliance and regional win-rates.
data.author: Khizar Nisar
data.full_text:
Selling across borders multiplies the chargeback problem in ways a single-market merchant rarely deals with: unfamiliar fraud patterns, different card network enforcement by region, and currency conversion disputes that domestic sellers never see. This roundup covers the international chargeback solutions cross-border ecommerce businesses are using in 2026 to keep disputes manageable across multiple markets at once.

Why cross-border chargebacks are a different problem than domestic ones

A merchant selling only within its home market builds up a fraud and dispute history that its tools, and its own instincts, can learn from over time. That history doesn’t transfer cleanly to a new market.

Currency fluctuations between the purchase date and the statement date generate their own category of disputes when a customer doesn’t recognize a slightly different charged amount. Shipping timelines are longer and less predictable across borders, which increases “item not received” disputes simply because customers wait longer and grow impatient sooner.

On top of that, Visa’s and Mastercard’s dispute-monitoring thresholds apply globally, but the practical risk tolerance and enforcement can vary by region and by the specific acquiring bank relationship in that market. A merchant expanding into three or four new countries at once can end up managing what amounts to three or four different risk profiles simultaneously, without three or four times the staff to handle it.

Best international chargeback solutions in 2026

1. Chargeflow

Chargeflow is built around a global operating model rather than a single-market one, supporting multi-store and multi-processor setups and reporting activity across 90 countries.

For a cross-border merchant, that breadth matters because the platform’s evidence-automation and prevention systems have been trained on dispute patterns across many markets rather than just one, which helps when a merchant is entering a country its own transaction history doesn’t cover yet.

On the prevention side, Chargeflow’s Alerts product connects to Visa and Mastercard’s dispute-alert networks, which operate consistently across markets even when local fraud behavior differs, catching a likely chargeback before it’s formally filed. The company reports Alerts can cut a merchant’s chargeback rate by up to 90% and begins working within 24 hours.

For disputes that do get filed, the platform automates evidence gathering and submission and reports a 100% submission rate, which matters across time zones and currencies where a manually tracked deadline is easy to miscalculate.

Pricing is success-based, meaning a merchant only pays when Chargeflow actually recovers a chargeback, with no long-term contract, which keeps costs proportional to actual dispute volume as a merchant scales into new markets rather than requiring a renegotiated flat fee each time.

The platform runs on SOC 2 Type 2 and GDPR-compliant infrastructure with data stored in US data centers, connects to more than 100 platforms including Shopify, Stripe, WooCommerce, and PayPal, and the company states it has recovered more than $200 million for merchants collectively.

Multi-store, multi-processor support built for cross-border operations

Prevention via Visa/Mastercard alert networks that work consistently across markets

Success-based pricing that scales cleanly as a merchant expands into new countries

2. Ethoca

Best for: merchants who want early visibility into Mastercard disputes across multiple markets.

Ethoca, run by Mastercard, connects merchants and issuing banks so a dispute can be resolved through a refund before it escalates into a formal chargeback, and it operates across Mastercard’s global network rather than being limited to specific regions.

Mastercard’s global merchant-issuer alert network

Refund-based resolution before formal chargebacks

Works consistently across the markets Mastercard operates in

3. Verifi

Best for: merchants who need the same early-warning coverage on Visa transactions internationally.

Verifi runs Visa’s Cardholder Dispute Resolution Network, alerting merchants to a likely dispute before it becomes a chargeback across Visa’s global footprint. Most cross-border merchants run Verifi and Ethoca together to cover both major networks internationally.

Real-time Visa dispute alerts across international markets

Refund window that avoids a formal chargeback being filed

Typically paired with Ethoca for full network coverage

4. ClearSale

Best for: merchants with significant order volume in Latin America or other markets where local review expertise helps.

ClearSale combines automated screening with a human review team, and its strongest coverage is in Latin American markets where local fraud patterns and documentation norms don’t always map cleanly onto a generic global model. That local expertise can matter more than raw model sophistication in specific regions.

Automated screening plus human manual review

Particularly strong Latin American market coverage

Useful where local fraud patterns differ from global norms

5. Riskified

Best for: merchants actively expanding into several new countries at once.

Riskified offers a chargeback guarantee on approved orders and draws on cross-merchant fraud data spanning many international markets, which helps most in the early stages of entering a country where the merchant’s own data is still thin.

Chargeback guarantee on approved international orders

Cross-merchant fraud intelligence across many markets

Strong fit during active multi-country expansion

6. Signifyd

Best for: merchants who want a financial guarantee alongside automated cross-border order decisions.

Signifyd reviews orders and backs its decisions with a guarantee against fraud-related chargebacks, which can offset some of the added uncertainty that comes with reviewing orders from markets a merchant is newer to.

Financial guarantee on approved orders

Automated order decisioning at checkout

Fee structure suited to higher international order volumes

7. Kount

Best for: merchants that need fraud prevention paired with identity verification across markets with different compliance rules.

Kount, an Equifax company, combines fraud detection with identity-verification tools, which helps merchants navigate the different know-your-customer and age-verification requirements that can vary significantly from one country to the next.

Fraud detection paired with identity verification

Backed by Equifax data and infrastructure

Useful where compliance requirements differ by market

8. Forter

Best for: merchants who want to minimize false declines on legitimate customers while expanding internationally.

Forter builds identity-trust profiles across its merchant network to make approve/decline decisions, with a stated focus on reducing false declines. That matters more in cross-border sales, where an unfamiliar billing address or device can look riskier to a generic model than it actually is for a legitimate customer.

Identity-based trust scoring shared across a global merchant network

Focus on reducing false declines for legitimate international customers

More common in larger, enterprise-scale cross-border implementations

9. Accertify

Best for: large merchants that want an enterprise-grade platform with deep regional configurability.

Accertify, owned by American Express, supports enterprise-level fraud and chargeback management with the configurability to tune rules differently by region, which suits a merchant with the internal resources to manage that complexity directly rather than relying on a vendor’s default global settings.

Deep, region-specific configurability

Backed by American Express infrastructure

Higher implementation effort, suited to larger cross-border operations

What cross-border merchants should check before choosing a provider

Data residency and compliance requirements should come first, before comparing features. Different markets have different rules about where transaction and cardholder data can be processed and stored, and that alone can rule out certain vendors before anything else gets evaluated.

From there, check whether a provider’s prevention model relies on network-level alerts tied to Visa and Mastercard, which behave consistently everywhere, or purely on its own proprietary fraud scoring built from its existing merchant base, since the second type tends to be less reliable in a market where neither the merchant nor the vendor has much transaction history yet.

Currency handling is a smaller but real detail worth checking too. A provider that clearly separates currency-conversion-related disputes from other reason codes in its reporting makes it much easier to spot when a specific market’s disputes are actually a currency-display problem on the checkout page rather than a fraud or fulfillment issue, which is a very different fix.

Language and local documentation norms matter more than most merchants expect going in.



A representment case built around US-style evidence conventions doesn’t always translate cleanly to how a dispute gets evaluated by an issuing bank in another region, and a provider with actual experience winning cases in a specific market tends to structure evidence differently for that market rather than submitting the same template everywhere.

That’s a harder thing to evaluate from a sales pitch alone, so asking a vendor directly about regional win-rate differences, not just a single blended number, is worth doing before committing.

Shipping and fulfillment partners add another wrinkle specific to cross-border sales. Longer transit times and customs delays both increase the odds of an “item not received” dispute simply because customers wait longer, and evidence requirements around proof of delivery can differ by destination country’s postal system.

A provider that automatically pulls tracking data at the carrier level, rather than requiring a merchant to manually attach it per case, saves real time once order volume across several countries starts adding up.

Frequently asked questions

Do chargeback rules differ significantly between countries?

The core Visa and Mastercard dispute frameworks apply globally, but practical enforcement, typical dispute reason codes, and risk tolerance can vary by region and by the specific acquiring bank relationship in that market.

Why do currency differences cause chargebacks?

A customer sometimes doesn’t recognize a charge on their statement if the converted amount differs from what they expected at checkout, due to exchange rate movement between the purchase and the statement date, which can lead them to dispute a legitimate transaction.

Should a cross-border merchant use multiple chargeback tools at once?

Many do, commonly pairing network-level alert services like Verifi and Ethoca with a broader platform that handles prevention and dispute automation together, since each layer addresses a different part of the problem across different markets.

How long does it typically take to see results after adding a prevention layer internationally?

Alert-based prevention tied to card networks can start flagging likely disputes within a day or two of setup, though a clear read on the overall impact to a merchant’s chargeback rate in a new market usually takes a month or two of data to assess properly.

data.ai_summary: AI image generation tools are enabling a surge in retail fraud and policy abuse, with 57% of merchants reporting increased refund and return scams. data.full_text:
AI is being pushed as a friend: your new sidekick that tackles the legwork you don’t have time for anymore. Great!

But what happens when you realize that this sidekick that helps is also scaling new ways that can directly hurt your business?

AI is both friend and foe in ways most consumers and brands are not prepared to handle.

Latest Videos From TechRadar Watch full video here:

Jason Grunberg Chief Marketing Officer at Forter.

Enter: AI imaging tools. These tools have become incredibly sophisticated and easily accessible, especially after recent upgrades. They can produce multiple high-quality images from a single prompt – no design background or expensive technology required.

The tools designed to help everyday users move quickly are now equally valuable to bad actors looking to make their schemes more convincing and harder to detect – and even consumers who feel pushed to abuse retail policies.

The age of AI-powered abuse is here: seeing should no longer be believing.

AI has democratized fraud

Businesses have long relied on photos and documentation to validate returns and refund requests. For a while, this logic was sound: the time, skill, and cost required to manufacture evidence acted as a barrier for most consumers, but the dam is breaking.

Are you a pro? Subscribe to our newsletter Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!

With modern image-generation tools, a malicious actor or your next-door neighbor doesn’t need design skills or specialist software. A single prompt can generate realistic receipts and damaged product images, turning the dial up on return abuse, refund fraud, and friendly fraud.

In fact, the Merchant Risk Council (MRC) found that over the past year, 57% of merchants reported increasing rates of refund and policy abuse. Retail’s global multi-billion-dollar fraud problem just became that much more costly, thanks to AI.

The speed and scale at which these images are produced, altered, and tested are staggering. With AI, fraudsters and abusers can now tailor claims to different merchants, test variations, and scale attacks across multiple accounts and thousands of merchants in short order.

The challenge is that AI-powered abuse is not being driven by one type of actor. Retailers are facing pressure from both organized fraud rings that deliberately exploit systems at scale and everyday consumers who are using new tools to push the boundaries of return and refund policies. While the motivations and sophistication levels are different, both create additional complexity for businesses trying to protect customers while preventing abuse.

Organized fraud groups are increasingly treating policy abuse as a scalable business model. Rather than relying on a single fraudulent claim, these groups look for weaknesses in retailer processes, create multiple accounts, and coordinate activity across merchants. AI-generated images make these operations more effective by providing convincing evidence that supports false claims, helping bad actors appear as genuine customers.

Forter has seen coordinated returns abuse operations where fraud rings used AI-altered images to support claims of product damage, including minor cracks, dents, and faulty components. In one case, Forter stopped a $1.5 million returns abuse operation over Christmas 2025 that used AI-altered damage images to make fraudulent refund requests appear legitimate. When not caught, these abusers resell the quality merchandise after getting refunded for the purchases.

The scale of these attacks is what makes them particularly challenging. A single suspicious claim may not reveal much, but when activity is connected across accounts, devices, behaviors, and merchants, a much bigger picture emerges. Fraud rings can spread activity across multiple retailers, making each individual interaction harder to identify without broader context.

AI has blurred the lines between fraud and abuse

But it’s not just organized criminals who are trying to cash in on these capabilities. The accessibility of AI image tools means everyday opportunistic shoppers are also starting to use them for their own gains. A shopper who wants to avoid the cost of a return, claim a refund for an item they damaged themselves, or take advantage of a flexible policy can now create realistic supporting evidence in seconds.

This creates a growing grey area for retailers. Not every questionable claim comes from a professional fraudster, and not every policy abuser operates with the same level of intent or organization. However, the impact is the same: businesses must spend more time and resources determining which return claims are from trusted customers and policy abusers, while legitimate customers risk facing additional friction as retailers respond to rising abuse.

Fighting AI with AI

Companies may be quick to tighten their policies to curb this AI-powered abuse. But shortening return windows, charging for returns, or delaying refunds reduces abuse at the expense of good customers. The goal has to be identifying the bad actor, not penalizing the good customer. Unfortunately, traditional measures like static rules and manual review processes can't operate at the speed or volume AI-powered fraud now demands.

Detection must operate across the full context – identity, device behavior, transaction history, account age, claim patterns – to catch what any individual piece of evidence would miss. Machine learning is the only realistic path to doing that at scale, in real time, without creating so much friction that legitimate customers are turned away.

Visual evidence needs to be augmented with commerce context and intelligence. A damaged phone screen from a long-term customer with one prior return means something very different than a three-day-old account submitting its fifth claim this week across dozens of retailers.

Businesses need to know with confidence who is behind the claim to assess what’s legitimate and what’s not.

Fraud prevention, insurance claims, cloud security, code generation. These are not experiments. What is notable is where competition concentrates at the infrastructure layer. Observability, data integration, and vector retrieval have become contested but necessary components of any serious AI deployment. The companies that establish themselves in those layers, Grafana Labs, Airbyte, and Qdrant among them, may not attract the same press attention as consumer-facing platforms, but their role in every production AI system gives them a durability that application-layer products have to earn repeatedly with each customer renewal. The next generation of enterprise AI contracts will be decided not just by which agent platforms win, but by which infrastructure layers become the default beneath them. Frequently Asked Questions What makes an AI company credible for enterprise use? Credible enterprise AI companies have production deployments with measurable outcomes, not just pilots. Look for companies with disclosed customer references, documented integration depth with existing systems, and a track record of handling edge cases in regulated environments. A genuinely enterprise-ready vendor can describe how their system fails gracefully and how errors surface to operators, not just how the product performs under ideal conditions.

How do enterprise teams evaluate AI vendors? Enterprise procurement teams typically assess AI vendors on four axes: data security and residency controls, integration depth with existing systems, pricing models that survive scaling, and escalation behavior when the model produces incorrect output. The last point is the one most vendors underestimate. Buyers want to understand what happens when the system is wrong, not just when it is right. Vendors that have clear answers to that question tend to have built their product for real operational conditions rather than demos. Which AI sectors are attracting the most enterprise investment in 2026? Customer service automation, code generation, and security analytics are drawing the most consistent enterprise spend. Healthcare AI is growing but still navigating compliance overhead that slows procurement cycles. Defense technology is accelerating, particularly for autonomous systems. Data infrastructure, including vector databases and integration platforms, is the quiet winner: it does not draw headlines but every serious AI deployment requires it, giving those vendors a structural position in almost every enterprise deal.

data.full_text:
Retailers are experiencing a sharp rise in AI-powered refund fraud, as shoppers and organised crime groups increasingly use generative AI tools to fabricate convincing return claims and exploit flexible retail policies.

© Silvabom | Dreamstime

According to new research from digital trust and fraud prevention platform Forter, AI-generated damage claims have become the fastest-growing form of return abuse. Fraudsters are now using widely available AI tools to create realistic fake evidence, including altered receipts, doctored images of damaged goods, and fabricated "item not received" narratives.

Forter warned that some coordinated fraud networks are scaling operations through "returns-as-a-service" models, where organised groups assist individuals in submitting fraudulent claims in exchange for a share of the profits. These tactics are evolving faster than many legacy fraud detection systems can respond.

Fashion retailers are particularly exposed due to high natural return rates, which already place pressure on margins and logistics. The data also shows that 53% of merchants report issues with "wardrobing", where customers wear clothing before returning it, while 30% of consumers admit to ordering extra items to meet free shipping thresholds and later returning them.

Overall, 44% of UK businesses say they are already affected by refund and returns abuse, with nearly half of retail leaders warning that the issue has become severe enough to consider scaling back operations or closing entirely.

Forter said the rise of generative AI is accelerating the sophistication and scale of fraud attempts, turning returns into a critical vulnerability in modern retail operations.

Source: www.meuble-info.fr

data.full_text:
JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor

Forter has launched five AI agents and opened early access to its Model Context Protocol, with the new products aimed at commerce teams handling fraud, payments, disputes and system integration. The rollout expands Forter Prism, the company's agent-based product suite, with tools focused on analytics, chargeback disputes, abuse prevention, payment approval rates and integration work. The agents are designed for specific workflows that merchant teams often handle manually. The Analytics Agent is intended to give users information on risk analysis, transactions, decision rationale, business performance and customer profiles. The Dispute Agent is aimed at automating chargeback disputes, while the Abuse Agent is designed to help merchants set policies around returns, promotions and loyalty misuse. The Payments Agent focuses on payment performance and recommendations intended to lift authorisation rates. The Integration Agent is designed to connect Forter with existing systems through an AI coding assistant that can reduce deployment time. Forter is also making early access available to its Model Context Protocol, or MCP. The system allows Forter's data to be used inside AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, so merchant teams can work with the information inside software they already use. According to Forter, the protocol lets teams analyse performance trends, investigate transactions and produce executive summaries without switching between separate systems. The same corporate permissions and security controls apply when data is used through those AI tools. The launch comes as merchants face pressure to make faster decisions at key points in the customer journey, including account sign-up, payment approval and post-purchase disputes. Fraud checks, payment issues and customer claims often require staff to gather information from several sources, slowing responses and affecting sales or customer experience. Forter said its products are built on a network of more than two billion shoppers and nearly one million merchants. That data network has become central to how the company positions its fraud and commerce decision tools to retailers and online businesses. AWS was among the outside companies quoted in support of the launch. "The merchants winning right now are the ones who can move from signal to action faster than their competitors, and that gap only grows," said Vince Koh, Global Head, AWS Digital Commerce. "Forter's agents ground fraud and revenue decisions in a network of two billion shoppers, giving commerce teams that edge." Forter has framed the launch as part of a wider shift in online commerce, where AI is changing how consumers discover products, interact with sellers and complete transactions. In turn, merchants must process more information in real time when deciding whether to approve orders, investigate activity or respond to disputes. Workflow focus The five agents map to functions that often sit across different teams. Analytics and payments tend to be handled by commercial and operations staff, disputes by finance or risk teams, and abuse prevention by fraud and customer experience teams. Integration work usually falls to technical teams responsible for connecting third-party software to internal systems. By separating the tools in this way, Forter is targeting practical operational tasks rather than offering a single general-purpose assistant. The approach reflects a broader shift in business software towards narrower AI systems built around defined jobs and data sources. Market pressure Payments and fraud vendors have been adding more AI-led products as merchants look for ways to reduce manual reviews, cut fraud losses and improve approval rates on legitimate transactions. Chargebacks and policy abuse have also become more expensive issues for retailers, especially in sectors with high volumes of returns and promotions. For companies already using large language model tools internally, the MCP element may be one of the more notable parts of the announcement. Rather than requiring staff to sign into a separate dashboard to query Forter data, the protocol is intended to bring that information directly into general AI interfaces already used for internal analysis. Eran Vanounou, Chief Technology Officer, Forter, said the aim was to make the company's data and decision tools easier to use in day-to-day work. "We've always built AI solutions for the people behind commerce who work tirelessly to offer the best experience to their consumers," said Eran Vanounou, Chief Technology Officer, Forter. "Intelligence is now accessible in seconds, in context, and with the accuracy our global network has built over 13 years. These AI agents create a competitive advantage for every Forter customer, who can now accelerate time to impact across the entire customer journey."
